item.title: Synology NAS Hole Rated 9.8 Opens Files Without a Password and Three DSM Versions Still Have No Fix
item.description:
Home NAS boxes from Synology can be opened over the network without a password, rated 9.8: files read, files overwritten. That is the factory setup. For DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1 and 7.1 there is still no fix. And attackers already use an old Synology NAS bug, CISA says.

A NAS is a box with hard drives that sits on your home or office network, often right next to the router. It keeps what the computers and phones around it should not lose: the photos from your phone, the backups of your laptop, scanned documents, shared folders. Synology makes these boxes, and the software on them is called DSM, short for DiskStation Manager. You log into it through a web page, and from there you manage the files, the users and the apps on the box.

# TL;DR

This week Synology warned about a hole in DSM with the number CVE-2026-120382. It got a score of 9.8 out of 10, and Synology put it in its highest category, Critical.

That score comes from a short line in the advisory: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N. Each part says something about the attack. It comes in over the network and is not hard to do, the attacker needs no account on your NAS, and you do not have to click or open anything for it to work. What the attacker gets, according to Synology, is your files to read, the possibility to write files onto the box, and the possibility to knock it offline.

Normally a warning like this comes with an update, but when Synology put this one online, the status said Ongoing and there was nothing to download yet. For DSM 7.4 and 7.3, Synology promised a fix by November 20. Two days later, DSM 7.2.2, DSM 7.2.1, DSM 7.1 and BeeStation OS 1.5, the system on Synology’s smaller home storage box, still have none. For 7.2.2 and 7.2.1, Synology’s advice is to move up to DSM 7.3. For DSM 7.1 and the BeeStation there is not even a date.

The technical part of the advisory goes back further than that table. It also names DSM 6.2, and it gives the build numbers that will carry the fix for the older versions: 6.2.4-25556-9, 7.1.1-42962-10, 7.2.1-69057-14 and 7.2.2-72806-11. Open Synology’s own download archive, where the company stores its DSM builds, and those builds are not there. The newest there are still 7.2.2-72806-10, 7.2.1-69057-13 and 7.1.1-42962-9.

For owners who cannot update, Synology has one piece of advice: switch off the package called OAuth Service. That is where the bug sits, in the part of DSM that handles OAuth.

OAuth is what happens when an app asks to use your account somewhere else. You know the screen: you sign in, and then you get the question whether this app may have access. You type your password at the service itself, never in the app, and the app gets a token back, a long string that says what it is allowed to do. OAuth Service does that for your NAS. Synology describes it as the package that lets you give apps from other companies access to DSM through those tokens, without sharing your login.

It is already on the box: in its own release notes, Synology calls OAuth Service a built-in package, from the very first version on October 5, 2017. A few months later, in March 2018, it was the part that let an Amazon Echo play music from Audio Station on the NAS when you asked it to. Since October 2025 the newer versions of the package need DSM 7.3 or higher, so a box on DSM 7.2 keeps running an older version of it.

What exactly breaks inside it, Synology does not say, and the advisory names no researcher. What it does give is the type of bug, and that tells a lot: CWE-88, Improper Neutralization of Argument Delimiters in a Command.

A program on the NAS builds a command for the operating system and puts something into it that came from outside, a username for example, or a value from a web request. That piece is supposed to be one word in the command. When the program does not check where that word ends, the person sending it can add words of their own: a space, two dashes, and an option the program never meant to offer.

Command-line tools are full of options like that. Take curl, the tool that downloads things from the web. With -o it saves the download to whatever path you put behind it, and with --config it reads its settings from a file you point it to. That is only an example of this type of bug, not Synology’s code, which has not been published. Slip one of those options into a command, and the tool reads or writes files for the attacker, with the rights of the service that runs it.

Nine days before, on November 10, Synology had already put out SA-26:19, also Critical, with two bugs in DSM. The first is an SQL injection in the part of DSM that handles logging in. It scored 9.8 as well, with the same result: files read and written and the box knocked offline, without an account. The second is a way past the login through rsync, the service DSM uses to copy files between machines, scored 8.6. Two researchers from the Viettel Cyber Security Research Lab and a researcher named Warisse Valentin found them.

And three seconds before the OAuth warning went online, Synology published another one, SA-26:20, which it called NGINX2Root, for CVE-2026-123007. NGINX is the web server software that DSM uses, and this bug is in the way it handles HTTP/2, the newer version of the protocol your browser uses to talk to websites. Under certain traffic, it writes past the end of a piece of memory, and the worker process usually crashes. On a system where ASLR, the protection that puts memory at random places, is switched off or can be bypassed, an attacker can run code. The score is 8.1.

The bug sits in that web server software itself. F5, the company behind it, published it on November 18 after four research teams reported it, and it goes back to version 1.9.5, so other servers that run it with HTTP/2 switched on have it too. One of those researchers, Stephen Fewer of Rapid7, has put proof-of-concept exploit code on GitHub. It runs code without a login against NGINX 1.31.8 in a test container, and according to his write-up it takes about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, roughly 17 minutes on a 1 Gbit/s connection. He built it for that test setup, not for DSM. On DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1 and 7.1 this bug is also still waiting for its fix.

Also on November 18, CISA, the US agency for cybersecurity, added four bugs to its list of bugs it has proof attackers are using. One of them is from Synology: CVE-2024-10441.

That bug comes from Pwn2Own 2024, a hacking contest where researchers break into devices for prize money and then hand the bugs to the makers. CVE-2024-10441 sits in a background service of DSM, scored 9.8 as well, and lets an attacker run code on the NAS without an account. Synology fixed it on November 5, 2024, for DSM 7.2.2. The fix for DSM 7.2 followed on February 11, 2025.

Two years later, the bug is being used in attacks, and that can only work on boxes that never got that update. The agency gave US federal agencies until November 21 to install the fix, or to stop using the product if they cannot. It also marked this bug for forensic triage, which means agencies have to look for signs that someone already got in. An update closes the hole, but it does not remove an attacker who is already inside.

Whether ransomware is involved, the agency marks as unknown. Synology had already said more, three weeks earlier. On October 29 it warned that attackers were using a vulnerability patched in December 2024 against boxes running an outdated DSM, to encrypt the data and demand a ransom. For the details, Synology pointed to SA-24:20, the same advisory that holds CVE-2024-10441. Which of the bugs in that advisory the attackers use, Synology does not say, and who is behind the attacks, neither of them says.

How a NAS can go two years without an update is partly explained in Synology’s own release notes. Above the smaller updates there is a note that your NAS may not tell you about them. Sometimes the update is not out in your region yet, because it rolls out in stages over a few days. And sometimes the system looks at its own services and settings and decides it does not need this update, and then you get no message at all.

For the big DSM releases it goes further. 48 older models get no update offered on the box. The owner has to go to Synology’s website and download it. And for 58 models, DSM 7.4 is the last version they can upgrade to.

The OAuth fix shows the same gap. For DSM 7.4 and 7.3 it came out on November 20 as 7.4.1-90080-2 and 7.3.2-86009-6, and Synology’s download archive has had a file for each model since that day. The release notes page still did not show either build on November 21, so an owner who checks there finds nothing new.

How many boxes can be reached from the internet with this hole has not been counted for this bug. Two years ago, the researchers at Midnight Blue looked at Synology boxes for a bug in Synology Photos. Shodan and Censys, two search engines that index devices on the internet, already showed hundreds of thousands of Synology NAS devices reachable from outside back then. The researchers estimated that one to two million boxes were reachable and had that Photos bug at the same time.

Those boxes were reachable through port forwarding, or through QuickConnect, Synology’s own service for getting to your NAS from outside. Port forwarding is a rule in your router that sends traffic from the internet straight to one device in your house. Set that up for the NAS, and the DSM login page is on the internet. For a bug that needs no account and no click, the box only has to be reachable.

Synology mentions no attacks with CVE-2026-120382 so far, and there is no public exploit code for it. For DSM 7.4 and DSM 7.3 the fix is out. For the other versions, switching off the package is the only protection against this bug.

What you can do right now:

  • → Check which DSM version your NAS runs: Control Panel, Info Center.

  • → On DSM 7.4 or 7.3: install 7.4.1-90080-2 or 7.3.2-86009-6, both out since November 20. If your NAS does not offer it, download the .pat file for your model from the Synology Download Center and install it under Control Panel, Update & Restore, Manual DSM Update. Until it is installed, stop OAuth Service as described below.

  • → On DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1 or 7.1: open Package Center, find OAuth Service and stop it. If an app or an Alexa skill can no longer sign in to your NAS after that, this is why. Start it again once your version has the fix. The same advice goes for BeeStation OS 1.5.

  • → For NGINX2Root: switch off HTTP/2 under Control Panel, Network, Connectivity. Stopping OAuth Service does nothing for that bug.

  • → Make sure the fix from 2024 is on the box: DSM 7.2.2-72806 Update 1 or later, 7.2.1-69057 Update 6 or later, or 7.2-64570 Update 4 or later.

  • → Look in your router for port forwarding rules that point to the NAS, usually ports 5000 and 5001. If you need the NAS from outside, reach it through a VPN instead of putting the login page on the internet. And switch off QuickConnect if you do not use it: for the Photos bug of 2024, the same researchers showed that QuickConnect made boxes reachable even without port forwarding.

Want to see what your NAS shows the internet? Look up your public IP on Shodan, or scan it with Nmap over mobile data.

item.title: nginx2root Chains a 2015 nginx HTTP/2 Bug and a Linux Kernel Zero-Day to Root, Even From Docker
item.description:
9.7 million web addresses announce an nginx version with a flaw that lets an attacker run code without logging in. HTTP/2 switched on is enough. The flaw went in with nginx’s first HTTP/2 code, in 2015.

nginx is the program on a server that answers when a browser asks for a web page. It sends the page itself, or it receives the request first and passes it on to other software behind it. According to the daily count of W3Techs, nginx runs 29.7 percent of the websites whose web server is known.

# TL;DR

On November 18, the nginx project released versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 with fixes for ten vulnerabilities. Five of them are memory bugs that the security company Xint found and named nginx2root. The most serious one is CVE-2026-123007, the public ID for a flaw in the part of nginx that speaks HTTP/2. F5, the company that owns nginx, gives it 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0, the scale used to score how serious a flaw is.

According to the researchers, an attacker who has no account on the server can make nginx execute commands of their choosing, as long as HTTP/2 is switched on. They showed it on a cloud server, attacking it from the outside over its public IP address. Then they used a second flaw, in the Linux kernel, and became root on the machine underneath. In that test, nginx ran inside a Docker container.

The scanning company Censys keeps a live count of nginx installations that are open to this flaw. On November 21, its tracker showed 9,776,434 services on an affected version with HTTP/2 switched on. It counts a service as an IP address or a hostname with a port, so one server can show up more than once. Another 114,417,159 nginx services hide their version number, and the company leaves those out. The tracker itself says the true number is higher.

About 3.7 million of the services in that count are distribution builds that name themselves in the server header, such as Ubuntu’s. Ubuntu fixes nginx without changing the version number, so many of those may already have the fix. The scanning company calls its count an estimate, not a check of each server.

The researchers did their own count on November 10, with Shodan, a search engine for devices on the internet. That search found 56.7 million hosts running nginx. 11.94 million of those showed a version number, and 98.9 percent of them fell in the affected range.

The only setting the flaw needs is HTTP/2, the newer way for a browser and a server to talk. With the older HTTP/1.1, a browser sends one request over a connection and waits for the answer before it sends the next one. HTTP/2 lets it send many requests over the same connection at once, each in its own numbered stream. In nginx, switching it on takes one word at the end of the line where a site listens for visitors: listen 443 ssl http2;. From version 1.25.1 on, it can also be a line of its own, http2 on;.

nginx got HTTP/2 in version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. The changelog for that release opens with the new module, ngx_http_v2_module, and thanks Dropbox and Automattic for sponsoring the work. The researchers found the vulnerable code in each official release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and in the development branch as it stood on November 10.

To keep one side from sending more than the other can handle, HTTP/2 keeps a counter on both ends. It says how much data the other side may still send, and it is called the flow control window. When the receiver has room for more, it sends a short message called WINDOW_UPDATE, and the window grows by the number in that message. The HTTP/2 standard sets a ceiling: the window may never go above 2,147,483,647 bytes, the largest number that fits in 31 bits.

The researchers found that a client can push the window for a connection past that ceiling. nginx has a check that should stop it. That check compares numbers that can never be negative, called unsigned numbers, and it does not see the overflow. From then on, nginx calculates with a window size that is wrong. It writes data outside the piece of memory it set aside, and it reads from outside it too. That memory is the heap, the pool the program hands out to itself while it runs.

The messages the attack uses to trigger the flaw are WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM, the second one telling the server to drop a stream. nginx does not log them as requests, and over HTTPS they are encrypted on their way in. An attack can leave little in the access log, the file where nginx writes down each visit.

Each time a program starts, its code and data land at a random place in memory, so an attacker does not know where to aim. That protection is called ASLR. F5 writes that an attacker can run code through this flaw when ASLR is off, or when they get around it. The researchers get around it by first using the same flaw to leak 64 bytes that hold addresses of the nginx program and of the heap.

The attacker’s commands then run as the nginx worker that handled the request. nginx starts one main process, and that process starts a few worker processes that deal with the visitors. A worker usually runs under a separate user with limited rights on the system. To get past those limits, the researchers used the second flaw.

That one sits in the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system, in its code for SCTP, a network protocol that runs next to the better known TCP and UDP. A connection in SCTP is called an association, and a program can hand an association over to another socket, the endpoint a program uses to send and receive. The researchers found that this handover can happen while a send on that association is still waiting. When the waiting send finishes, it frees the association, while the other socket still uses it. Depending on what that socket does next, the kernel uses memory that was already given back, or gives the same memory back twice.

That bug gives the researchers two things. The first is a leak of kernel memory that defeats KASLR, the same random placement for the kernel itself. The second is a way to make the kernel call a function the attacker picks. In their tests, an attacker already running code as an nginx worker could reliably become root. The kernel flaw went into Linux in version 4.15, in 2018. When the researchers published, it had no CVE and no patch, and they are holding back most of the details until a fix is out.

On many Linux distributions, they write, the SCTP module is installed by default, and the kernel loads it on its own the first time a program opens an SCTP socket. Code running in the nginx worker can open one and bring the vulnerable code into the kernel. On a given host, it depends on the kernel, the modules on it and the limits set on the container, they add. Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 and later is an exception: there, SCTP comes in a separate package, kernel-modules-extra, and the company writes that the module is blacklisted by default.

This is why Docker did not stop it. A container has its own files and its own processes, but it runs on the kernel of the host, the same kernel the other containers on that machine use. Root in that kernel means control over the host and over the other containers on it. The researchers do not say which Docker settings the test container ran with.

They tested the nginx flaw on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure: from inside the server, from the private network next to it, and over the public IP address. They list success in each of those nine tests, and write that the attack also works with normal traffic on the server at the same time.

It is the second SCTP flaw this year that leads out of a container. In August, Tencent’s Zhuque Lab published CVE-2026-64564, a different bug in the kernel’s SCTP code, and reached root on the host in six of eight attempts from inside a container. That test kept the default seccomp profile switched on, the filter that blocks risky system calls inside a container, and gave the container none of the extra rights CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Linux has fixed that one.

The nginx2root researchers were not the only team on this bug. They reported their five bugs to F5 on October 16. One of them had found the flow control flaw first, and a few days later an automated scan by the same company found the other four without a person guiding it. F5’s advisory thanks four teams for the flow control flaw, and next to one of them, Ikotas Labs, it names GPT-6 Astra, an AI model.

Wiz Research lists five teams that found the HTTP/2 flaws separately, its own among them. It found its two with Atlas, the system behind its AI code scanning. Its date is November 11, 12:16 UTC, a week before the release and the advisory. The commit does not show the moment it became visible there. On that same November 11, Rapid7, where Stephen Fewer had found the same flaw, made its first contact with F5 about it and sent its report the next day.

He also published an exploit for the nginx flaw: code that runs commands on a vulnerable nginx 1.31.8 in a Docker image for 64-bit Linux, with HTTP/2 and HTTPS switched on. His write-up puts the traffic it needs at about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s connection, seventeen minutes on 1 Gbit/s. On a line slower than about 300 Mbit/s it does not finish, because nginx closes a connection after one hour by default. The nginx2root researchers kept the last steps of their own exploit out of their write-up, and write that their approach does not depend on exact response sizes.

Seven days before the nginx release, on November 11, the Apache project published a critical flaw in its HTTP/2 module that can also lead to remote code execution. The same daily count puts that web server at 20.4 percent of the websites with a known web server, and nginx at 29.7. Within one week, the two web servers behind about half of those websites both got an HTTP/2 flaw that can let an attacker run code.

nginx is also built into other F5 products. The advisory lists the NGINX Ingress Controller, which brings outside traffic into a Kubernetes cluster, with fixes in version 5.8.0 and in its long-term support release 2026-lts-r11. For its 4.x and 3.x lines, for NGINX App Protect WAF, NGINX App Protect DoS, NGINX Gateway Fabric 1.x and NGINX Plus R34 to R36, it lists no fixed version. Under mitigation, it says none.

So far, no attacks using these flaws have been reported. The scanning company knew of none on November 18, and Cloudflare had seen no reports on November 19, though it warns that fake exploits for nginx2root are going around on GitHub. CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, had not added any of the five to its catalog of exploited flaws by then.

The fix is nginx 1.31.9 or 1.30.7, and NGINX Plus 37.3.0.1 or 37.0.8.1. Older nginx branches get no fix from the project, so a server on one of them has to move up.

Since November 18, the tracker has seen 11,067,818 services on an affected version with HTTP/2 switched on. By November 21, 1,236,068 of them had updated or switched HTTP/2 off, 183,355 of those in the last 24 hours. A fixed service only shows up as fixed after its next scan, so the count runs a few days behind.

The most common version on the tracker is 1.24.0, the nginx that comes with Ubuntu 24.04. Linux distributions put the fix into their own packages and keep the old number, which is called backporting. Debian and RHEL do the same, but their servers do not name themselves in the header, so a fixed one still counts as exposed on the tracker.

Where the distributions stand:

  • → Ubuntu published its notice on November 19, with fixes from 16.04 through 26.10. Versions 20.04 and older get theirs through Ubuntu Pro
  • → The fixed Ubuntu package is 1.18.0-6ubuntu14.23 on 22.04, 1.24.0-2ubuntu7.20 on 24.04 and 1.28.3-2ubuntu1.13 on 26.04
  • → Debian fixed version 13 (trixie) with 1.26.3-3+deb13u11 and version 12 (bookworm) with 1.22.1-9+deb12u11

A configuration reload keeps the old program running, so nginx has to be restarted after the update.

These commands show which version runs, if nginx has HTTP/2 built in, and where the configuration switches it on. On Debian or Ubuntu, the last one shows the package version to compare with the list above:

1
2
3
4

nginx -v
nginx -V 2>&1 | grep -o with-http_v2_module
grep -rn "http2" /etc/nginx/
dpkg -l nginx | grep ^ii

A server that cannot update yet can switch HTTP/2 off, which blocks this flaw and the other HTTP/2 flaw. From version 1.25.1 on, that means http2 off; in each server block and no http2 on the listen lines. On older versions, take http2 out of the listen line. Then test the configuration and restart:

1
2
3
4

listen 443 ssl;
http2 off;
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl restart nginx

For the kernel flaw, the researchers advise stopping the SCTP module from loading, which also takes SCTP away from programs that use it. That does not unload a module that is already loaded, and it does nothing on a kernel with SCTP built in. The first command shows if it is loaded:

1
2

lsmod | grep sctp
echo "install sctp /bin/false" | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/disable-sctp.conf

The update fixes the flaw, but it does not show if an attacker already used it. Because the attack can leave so little in the access log, the researchers describe other places to look.

The first is the connection itself. During an attack, one connection from the same address stays open for minutes, and the number of bytes nginx receives on it keeps climbing fast while nginx sends little back. That is the flood of WINDOW_UPDATE messages. Run this command twice, a short time apart, and compare bytes_received and bytes_sent:

1

sudo ss -tinp state established '( sport = :443 )'

The second is a log that also records which connection each request came over and how many requests that connection carried. It goes in the http block of the nginx configuration. When the bytes received keep growing while the logged requests stay small, the client is sending data that never shows up as a request:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9

log_format h2_hunt '$time_iso8601 src=$remote_addr conn=$connection '
                   'requests=$connection_requests proto=$server_protocol '
                   'status=$status request_length=$request_length '
                   'bytes_sent=$bytes_sent request_time=$request_time';
access_log /var/log/nginx/h2-hunt.log h2_hunt;
sudo nginx -t && sudo nginx -s reload
sudo grep 'proto=HTTP/2.0' /var/log/nginx/h2-hunt.log | tail -n 200

The third is a program started by the worker. A normal nginx worker has no reason to run other programs, and the researchers’ exploit starts a shell through execve(), the system call that starts a program. According to the researchers, a program started by an nginx worker is the clearest sign of a successful attack. The first command shows the user ID the workers run under. On systems with auditd, the Linux audit system, the rule after it logs each program started under that ID, with NGINX_UID replaced by that number:

1
2
3

ps -eo uid,user,pid,ppid,args | grep '[n]ginx: worker process'
sudo auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve,execveat -F euid=NGINX_UID -k nginx_worker_exec
sudo ausearch -k nginx_worker_exec -ts recent -i

With -ts recent, ausearch only looks back ten minutes, and -ts today covers the day. The rule only records what happens after it is added, so an empty result does not rule out an earlier break-in. It also catches other processes under the same user ID, so the process and parent process IDs tell which entries came from nginx.

The fourth is a worker that crashed. A failed attempt can bring a worker down, and so can problems that have nothing to do with an attack:

1
2

sudo grep -Ei 'worker process.*exited|signal 11|segfault' /var/log/nginx/error.log
sudo coredumpctl list nginx

On their own, high incoming traffic, many connections from one address, a gap between bytes received and logged requests, and crashed workers can each have a normal cause. When several of them show up together and there is no explanation, the researchers advise blocking the source and investigating.

Run curl -sI --http2 against a server you own and check whether it answers over HTTP/2 and which nginx version it announces.

3

3

3
4
5
6
7
8

item.title: BYOD Hackers Locked a Trauma Center's Computers, Then Offered Patients 2,500 Dollars
item.description:
For two hours, New Mexico’s only trauma center sent its ambulances to other hospitals. Its own computers were reading a ransom demand out loud. The next day the hackers said sorry, and kept the data.

# TL;DR

It started on a Monday morning, October 26, at the university hospital in Albuquerque. Around 11 o’clock, the hospital’s IT team saw something on the network that did not belong there and started shutting it out. A little after noon, the staff got an alert to unplug their desktops and switch off WiFi on their phones.

Then the computers started to talk.

A computer voice, the flat kind that text-to-speech software makes, came out of the machines inside the hospital. A local TV station got part of the recording. The voice said the attackers had the data of the students and employees, their Social Security numbers, their private documents and their email. It told the people in charge to get in touch right away, through an encrypted chat app called Session, or the university would be taken down so far it could no longer function. On the screens, a red skull appeared with the words “Oh no, you have been compromised.” A doctor at the hospital told the student newspaper that the message played on their own computer.

This hospital is the only Level 1 trauma center in New Mexico. Level 1 is the highest level of trauma care, the hospital where the most badly injured patients are taken. The same health system runs the only burn unit and the only children’s hospital in the state, and it takes care of a large part of the people in New Mexico who have no health insurance. In a normal year, it handles around 900,000 outpatient visits and 100,000 visits to the emergency room.

From 12:30 to 2:30 that afternoon, the hospital sent its ambulances to other hospitals in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. For those two hours, a patient in New Mexico with the worst kind of injury had no emergency room in the state that could take them. The hospital cancelled the appointments at more than 30 clinics for the rest of the day and stopped the outpatient surgeries. Patients were told to stay home, to call 911 if it was an emergency, and to wait with the rest.

That same day, the attackers put the university on their website.

They call themselves BYOD. Like many ransomware groups, they run a leak site, a website on the Tor network where they list the organizations they hit and publish the stolen data of the ones that do not pay. Their post about the university was loud. It claimed 36,000 computers and both of the university’s Active Directory networks, one for the campus and one for the hospital. Active Directory is how a big organization decides who you are when you log in, and which computers and files you may use. The post also claimed the cloud version of that system, two Oracle databases, the payroll, the student records and the internal email. It would come down, the group wrote, once the university got in touch.

The hospital tells a much smaller story. Its own investigation found that some of the computers people work on were hit, but that the attackers did not get into the core systems or the servers. Two days later, some employees still had to leave their computers off.

Then, on the Tuesday, the hackers changed their tone.

In a post titled “UPDATE: UNM,” the group wrote that it had not known those machines were helping patients while they were being treated. It offered the key for the remaining locked computers for free, but only on the hospital side. The campus stayed locked.

In brackets, the group added that it would have kept the hospital locked too if those machines had only held appointments, patient information and research data. So the apology covered the machines that helped patients during treatment. And then it spoke to the patients themselves. A patient who was affected could send proof, and the group would pay them up to 2,500 dollars each, for the inconvenience. It wrote that it was sorry, that it had morals and a heart, and that it was not a villain. In the same post, it wrote that it would keep the data, and that it would go on holding companies responsible for bad security.

That free key gave something away. You can only hand out a key for computers you have locked.

Look at that 2,500 dollar offer from the patient’s side. To get the money, you would have to prove who you are, to the people who took your medical records.

The hospital answered on Wednesday. Without naming the group, it said it had made no deals with the people behind the attack. It warned that they might now go after patients, students and employees one by one, with false offers of payment or compensation. It told them not to answer, and to keep the message and report it to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Two weeks later, the same voice turned up in Nashville, Tennessee.

On Monday, November 9, around 8:30 in the morning, Vanderbilt University started fighting off an attack. The university has about 14,000 students. At 10:45, it sent a message to its students and staff: shut down your university devices, get off the campus WiFi, and watch out for these signs:

  • → pop-ups and security warnings that come out of nowhere

  • → files that move, change or disappear

  • → programs you did not install

  • → a request to type in your password or approve a login that you did not start yourself

A professor’s laptop played the voice in the middle of a class, the university’s own student newspaper reported, and a video of it went online. This is what it said:

“You have been compromised by BYOD. We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one.”

On the desktop sat a file called README_BYOD_31.txt with the instructions. On their leak site, the group claims it locked the university’s databases and took over the domain controller, the server that holds the accounts and passwords for the network. It also claims research data and more than one million Social Security numbers. The university has not confirmed any of that.

It has said how far from over this is. On November 19, ten days in, the university still called it an ongoing cyberattack. OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams and Copilot were still switched off. The files in Box came back that day, set back to how they were right before 8:30 on November 9. The first step to bring OneDrive back is planned for the first week of December. So many laptops were hit that the university emails their owners in daily batches, and for desktop computers and shared machines it is still working on a fix.

The group claims far more than two schools. TrendAI Research counted at least nine organizations in the five weeks between October 5 and November 9, and the researchers keep apart what the victims confirmed and what the group claims. Here is what the group put on its leak site, and what it says it has:

  • → October 5: Trump Mobile. The names, home addresses, email addresses, phone numbers and order details of 3,615 customers went online, including people who never finished signing up. People in the data confirmed it was theirs. A member of the group later claimed they got in through malware on the computer of an employee at the mobile carrier that runs the service.

  • → October 13: Decorolala, a Canadian home goods shop. The group claims 60,544 customers, with home addresses down to the exact coordinates, and the UPS tracking links of their orders. According to the group, those links include delivery photos of the outside of the customers’ houses.

  • → November 2: Michigan State University. The group claims the personal data of 1.03 million current and former students, plus their current and old passwords. On November 16, it posted that data for download.

  • → November 4: IHG Hotels & Resorts, the company behind Holiday Inn, Crowne Plaza and Staybridge Suites. The group claims guest names, billing addresses, room charges, stay dates and the loyalty program data. It also mocked the company for a directory password of 123, and claims full access to CyberArk, the vault where the company keeps its most powerful passwords. The next day came a post titled “First and Final Warning,” with sample files.

  • → November 9: the Texas Health and Human Services Commission, the agency that runs Medicaid and food assistance in the state. The group claims data on 2 million Texans, including health, food aid and bank details. A “final warning” with a sample followed on November 16.

  • → November 10: Toyota in Japan. The group claims names, email addresses, home addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and access to kiosk devices.

The hotel chain, the carmaker and the Texas agency have not confirmed an incident, and the agency told reporters the claims are unverified.

One group hit a trauma center and two universities in five weeks, and claims a hotel chain and a state agency. A known software flaw gets an official number, a CVE. No CVE has been tied to a BYOD attack. That also means there is no patch you can install against this group.

The trail points to logins. The university in Michigan saw suspicious activity that looked like stolen passwords. On October 1, it made the holders of a university account pick a new password of at least 15 characters. A month later, the group listed it. And then there is that password of 123 at the hotel chain, if the group is telling the truth.

That same hotel company’s password vault came up four years ago. In 2022, the hackers behind an earlier attack on it said in an interview that they got into the vault with the password Qwerty1234, and that the login for it was visible to 200,000 staff. The company disputed that its vault was insecure.

Ransomware.live, a site that tracks ransomware groups, also shows data on infostealers: small programs that copy the saved passwords and login cookies out of a browser and send them to the attacker. That data comes from Hudson Rock, a company that follows them. For the BYOD victims with a known web domain, 100 percent had staff or users whose logins were stolen this way. For that university in Michigan alone, the tracker counts 624 employees and 3,674 users.

With a working password, the attacker logs in as that person. From there, the group keeps naming the same targets: Active Directory, the domain controller, and Group Policy, the part of Windows an administrator uses to send settings and scripts to the computers in a network from one place. Get control of that, and you can push your own program to those computers in one go. That is how many ransomware groups lock an organization in one step.

Access like that also fits the voice. To play sound on many computers at once, the attackers had to be able to run their own code on many computers at once. The researchers say that matches the wide access BYOD claims, without proving it.

The warning list from Nashville points the same way. A login request you did not start and permissions on your cloud files that suddenly changed are the signs of someone walking around with a stolen account.

BYOD first showed up in September 2026. On its leak site it calls its work “pentesting,” meant to expose bad security and to hold accountable the organizations that see their customers as a number. The name is the same as the IT term “bring your own device,” but the group has never explained it.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. What we know for sure is what the victims confirmed and what the group posted. Who is behind BYOD, nothing public answers yet.

In Albuquerque, the ambulances were back at 2:30 that Monday afternoon. By Tuesday afternoon, the hospital reported its critical systems back online and the clinics open again. The hospital says it did not pay. At the end of October, it was still waiting for the forensic results to know whether patient data was taken. In Nashville, getting the systems back will take weeks.

What you can do:

  • → Someone contacts you and says they have your data, with a threat or with an offer of money. Do not answer, do not click and do not pay. Keep the message and report it. In the US that is IC3.gov.

  • → Never approve a login request on your phone that you did not start yourself. A string of those prompts means someone already has your password.

Want to see what one stolen login would let an attacker reach on your own network? Map your home network with Nmap from a second machine and find out.

item.title: GL.iNet Cloud Flaw Gave Attackers Root on Routers and KVMs Through a Feature That Was Switched Off
item.description:
Routers and KVMs took root commands and malware from the maker’s own cloud, with signs on 166 of 199 routers one firm checked. Owners had the abused feature turned off. The hole was 715 days old.

GL.iNet makes small travel routers that fit in a jacket pocket, the kind you take along on a trip. You plug one in at a hotel or a holiday rental, and your laptop and phone go through your own little network instead of straight onto the hotel WiFi. The company also makes home routers, and a line of KVM devices called Comet.

# TL;DR

A KVM over IP is a small box that you plug into the HDMI and USB ports of a computer. From your browser you then see that computer’s screen and use its keyboard and mouse as if you were sitting in front of it, even while it is still starting up. That is handy when the computer is a server in a closet, or your work PC at the office while you are at home.

To manage those devices from wherever you are, GL.iNet has a cloud service called GoodCloud. You link your router or KVM to your account, and from that moment on the device keeps a connection open to GL.iNet’s servers and waits for instructions. You change a setting in the app, the cloud sends a message down that connection, and your device does what the message says.

On the KVMs, that cloud service is switched on by default, GL.iNet’s own documentation says so. And according to the company’s security notice, some KVMs already had it running before their owner had even linked them to an account.

So the device listens to the cloud. On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet announced that someone had used a hole in that cloud to put malware on routers and KVMs of its customers.
